summary: Defines the IMAP METADATA extension, which lets clients and servers keep annotations on mailboxes or on the whole server, such as a comment on a mailbox's purpose or a message of the day. This is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: IMAP is the protocol a mail client uses to talk to a mail server. This extension lets a client attach small named notes to a mailbox or to the whole server, the way a sticky note records something about a folder. A note can be private to one user or shared with everyone who is allowed to see it.

how to set a comment on an imap mailbox
subtitle: Sticky notes for IMAP: named annotations attached to a mailbox, or to the whole server.

tldr.problem: IMAP clients had no standard way to store small pieces of data, such as a comment about what a mailbox is for, or a server-wide message of the day.
tldr.mechanism: The METADATA extension adds the GETMETADATA and SETMETADATA commands and a METADATA response, working on slash-separated entry names such as /shared/comment and /private/comment.
tldr.outcome: Clients and servers can share per-mailbox and server-wide annotations, with private entries kept per user and shared entries visible to authorized users.

today: RFC 5464 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata records no obsoleting or updating document, so it remains the definition of the IMAP METADATA extension, adding two commands and one response to the base IMAP protocol.

sections.title: Introduction and Overview
sections.content:
The goal of the METADATA extension is to provide a means for clients to set and retrieve annotations, also called metadata, on an IMAP server. The annotations can be associated with specific mailboxes or with the server as a whole. A server may support only server annotations, or both server and mailbox annotations.

A server that supports both server and mailbox annotations advertises the extension by returning METADATA as one of the supported capabilities in the CAPABILITY command response. A server that supports only server annotations returns METADATA-SERVER instead. A server that sends unsolicited annotation change responses MUST support the RFC 5161 ENABLE extension so that clients can turn that feature on.

The extension makes four changes to the IMAP base protocol: it adds a SETMETADATA command, a GETMETADATA command, a METADATA untagged response, and a METADATA response code. The rest of the document defines the data model behind those four pieces and the protocol changes in detail.
sections.plainLanguage: A server that supports this extension says so when the client asks what it can do. The client can then read and write short named notes attached to a folder or to the server as a whole. If the server supports both kinds of note, it announces one capability name; if it only supports server-wide notes, it announces another.

sections.title: The Annotation Data Model
sections.content:
Mailboxes, or the server as a whole, may have zero or more annotations associated with them. An annotation contains a uniquely named entry, which has a value. Annotations are added to a mailbox when a mailbox name is given as the first argument to SETMETADATA, and to the server as a whole when the empty string is given as the first argument. For example, a general comment added to a mailbox may have the entry name /comment and the value Really useful mailbox.

The value of an entry is either NIL, meaning it has no value, or a string or binary data of zero or more octets. A string MAY contain multiple lines of text, and clients MUST use the CRLF character octet sequence to represent line ends in a multi-line string value.

The protocol changes allow a client to access or change the values of any annotation entry, assuming it has sufficient access rights to do so.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note has a name and a value, and the value can be empty, text, or binary data. Text can run over several lines. A note belongs either to one named folder or to the whole server, and the empty server name is how the command says which one it means.

sections.title: Entry Names, Scopes and Who May Change Them
sections.content:
Each annotation is an entry with a hierarchical name, each component separated by a slash. An entry name MUST NOT contain two consecutive slash characters and MUST NOT end with a slash. Entry names MUST NOT contain asterisk or percent characters, non-ASCII characters, or characters with octet values in the range 0x00 to 0x19; an invalid entry name results in a BAD response in any IMAP command in which it is used. Entry names are case-insensitive, and the use of control or punctuation characters in them is strongly discouraged.

The first component of an entry name defines its scope. Only the prefixes /private and /shared are defined. A private annotation is stored on a per-user basis and is not visible to other users. A shared annotation has a single value that can be read and changed by authorized users with appropriate access. Entry names can have any number of components starting at 2, unless they fall under the vendor namespaces /shared/vendor/<vendor-token> or /private/vendor/<vendor-token>, in which case they have at least 4 components. The vendor token MUST be registered with IANA using the ACAP vendor subtree registry.

Entry names MUST be specified in a Standards Track or IESG-approved Experimental RFC, or fall under the vendor namespace. The names this document defines are /shared/comment and /shared/admin for the server, and /shared/comment and /private/comment for a mailbox. The /shared/admin entry holds a way to contact the server administrator, its value MUST be a URI, and it is always read-only, so clients cannot change it.
sections.plainLanguage: Names are written like file paths, starting with either /private or /shared. That first part says who can see the note: only you, or everyone with permission. This document defines four names: a comment for the server, an administrator contact for the server, a comment for a folder, and a private comment for a folder. Vendors can add their own names under a registered prefix.

sections.title: Reading Annotations with GETMETADATA
sections.content:
GETMETADATA retrieves server or mailbox annotations. It is only available in authenticated or selected state. It takes a mailbox name, options and an entry specifier, and returns a required METADATA response. An empty mailbox name means server annotations; a non-empty name means the annotations on that mailbox. Entry specifiers can be lists of atomic specifiers, so several annotations may be returned in one command.

Two options are defined. The MAXSIZE option restricts which values come back: only values less than or equal to the limit in octet size are returned. If any requested entry has a value larger than the limit, the server MUST include the METADATA LONGENTRIES response code in the tagged OK response, giving the size of the biggest entry value requested that exceeded the limit.

The DEPTH option extends the list of values returned. For each entry name given, the server returns the value of that entry if it exists, plus all entries below it up to the stated depth. Three values are allowed: 0 for no entries below the specified entry, 1 for only entries immediately below it, and infinity for all entries below it. If DEPTH is not specified, that is the same as specifying DEPTH 0. So DEPTH 1 for an entry /a matches /a and its children such as /a/b, but not grandchildren such as /a/b/c.
sections.plainLanguage: The read command names a folder, or nothing at all for the server as a whole, and lists the notes it wants. Two options control how much comes back. MAXSIZE drops notes whose value is too large and tells the client the size of the biggest one it dropped. DEPTH reaches down the name tree: depth 0 gets only the names you asked for, depth 1 also gets the ones directly below, and infinity gets everything below.

sections.title: Writing Annotations with SETMETADATA
sections.content:
SETMETADATA sets annotations. It is only available in authenticated or selected state. It sets the specified list of entries by adding or replacing the values given, on the specified existing mailboxes or on the server if the mailbox argument is the empty string. Clients can use NIL for the value of an entry they want to remove. The server SHOULD NOT return a METADATA response containing the updated annotation data, and clients MUST NOT assume that one will be sent; they MUST assume that if the command succeeds, the annotation has been changed.

Three failures have their own response codes. If a value is too large, the server MUST return a tagged NO response with a [METADATA MAXSIZE NNN] response code, where NNN is the maximum octet count it will accept. If the maximum number of annotations has been reached, it MUST return [METADATA TOOMANY]. If it cannot support private annotations on one of the specified mailboxes, it MUST return [METADATA NOPRIVATE]. When any one annotation fails to be set, the server MUST NOT change the values for the other annotations named in the same command.

The server is allowed to impose limits on the size of any one annotation or on the total number of annotations for a mailbox or for the server as a whole, but it MUST accept an annotation data size of at least 1024 bytes and an annotation count per server or mailbox of at least 10.
sections.plainLanguage: The write command takes a folder or the server, then pairs of names and values. Sending an empty value removes a note. Several notes can be set in one command, and if any one of them fails, none of them are changed. The server explains a refusal with one of three codes: the value was too big, too many notes already exist, or private notes are not supported there.

sections.title: The METADATA Response
sections.content:
The METADATA response displays the results of a GETMETADATA command, and can also be returned as an unsolicited response at any time by the server in response to a change in a server or mailbox annotation. When unsolicited responses are activated by the ENABLE command for this extension, servers MUST send unsolicited METADATA responses if server or mailbox annotations are changed by a third party, which lets servers keep clients updated with changes.

Unsolicited METADATA responses MUST only contain entry names, not the values. If the client wants to update any cached values, it must retrieve them explicitly with GETMETADATA. A response can contain multiple entries in a single response, but the server is free to return multiple responses for each entry or group of entries. This response is only available in authenticated or selected state.
sections.plainLanguage: The server answers a read with the names and values you asked for. It can also send the same response on its own when someone else changes a note. When it does that it sends only the names, not the values, so the client has to ask again if it wants the new text.

sections.title: Registering New Entries
sections.content:
All entries MUST have either /shared or /private as a prefix, and entry names MUST be specified in a Standards Track or IESG-approved Experimental RFC, or fall under the vendor namespace. Each entry registration MUST include a content type that indicates the nature of the annotation value, and a charset parameter MUST be included with the content type where applicable.

The registration template asks for the type, either Mailbox or Server, the name of the entry, a description of what the entry is for, the MIME content type and charset for the entry value, the RFC number for entries published as RFCs, and a contact. This document registers four entries itself: the server entries /shared/comment and /shared/admin, and the mailbox entries /shared/comment and /private/comment. All four use the content type text/plain; charset=utf-8.
sections.plainLanguage: New note names are not free-for-all: they need a Standards Track document, or they need to sit under a registered vendor prefix. When one is registered, IANA records whether it belongs to a folder or to the server, what it is for, and what kind of value it holds.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations in Section 11 of RFC 3501 apply with respect to protecting annotations from snooping. Servers MAY choose to support the METADATA and METADATA-SERVER extensions only after a privacy layer has been negotiated by the client.

Annotations can contain arbitrary data of varying size, so servers MUST ensure that size limits are enforced, to prevent a user from using up all available space on a server and preventing use by others. Clients MUST treat annotation data values as an untrusted source of data, since it is possible for it to contain malicious content.

Annotations whose values are intended to remain private MUST be stored only in entries that have the /private prefix on the entry name. Excluding these issues, the METADATA extension does not raise any security considerations that are not already present in the base IMAP protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Notes are as visible to an eavesdropper as the rest of the session, so a server may only offer the extension once the connection is protected. Notes can hold any data of any size, so the server must cap how much one user can store, and the client must treat what it reads as untrusted, because a note could contain an attack. Anything meant to stay secret has to go under the /private prefix.

items.label: Value too large
items.desc: The server returns this with a tagged NO response, where NNN is the maximum octet count it will accept.

items.label: Too many annotations
items.desc: The server has already reached the maximum number of annotations on the named mailbox.

items.label: Private not supported
items.desc: The server cannot support private annotations on one of the specified mailboxes.

items.label: Value dropped by MAXSIZE
items.desc: The server returns this in the tagged OK response of a GETMETADATA, with the size of the biggest entry value that exceeded the limit.
